extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing tragic drama: how to construct the plot, shape character, handle recognition and reversal, and use diction, metaphor, and the chorus to produce pity and fear. Emphasis on unity of action, appropriate incidents, and stylistic moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (single action)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well constructed plot should be single in its issue; the plot should have a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid multiplicity of plots or an Epic structure in drama (e.g., dramatizing the whole Iliad or the whole Fall of Troy). The plot should resemble a living organism in its unity and produce its proper pleasure. Examples: Homer detaches a single portion and admits episodes; tragedy should not attempt the entire war of Troy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune (reversal) — good to bad
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should be not from bad to good, but, reversely, from good to bad, and should come about not by vice but by some great error or frailty in the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist ought to be one 'not eminently good and just' but renowned and prosperous so that his misfortune arises from error or frailty (peripeteia). This produces true tragic effect; plays ending unhappily on this principle are rightly tragic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of catastrophe — error or frailty, not vice
rubrics_metrics.description: The disaster should result from some great error or frailty rather than from vice or depravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select protagonists whose misfortune can be traced to an error/weakness (e.g., Oedipus) rather than moral wickedness; this elicits pity and fear properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoking pity and fear from the plot (not spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means, but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way and indicates a superior poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidents so that hearing the tale (without spectacle) thrills with horror and melts to pity. Relying on spectacle risks producing a sense of the monstrous rather than the tragic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of tragic incidents — relation between persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity or terror must happen between persons who are friends, near, or dear to one another (e.g., brother and brother, son and father).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidents between enemies or indifferent persons arouse less pity (except for suffering itself). Poets should seek stories from families whose histories contain moving incidents of kinship and betrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) — kinds and hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition has several kinds: by signs/tokens, by poet-invented revelation, by memory/feeling, by process of reasoning, and the best is that which arises from the incidents themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rankings and examples: (1) recognition by signs (least artistic; e.g., scars, tokens), (2) invented revelations (lacking art), (3) memory/feeling awakened by an object (e.g., a picture or music), (4) reasoning/inference, (best) natural recognition arising from incident (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigenia). Prefer recognitions that dispense with artificial tokens and grow from the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and unravelling (structural partition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy falls into two parts—Complication and Unravelling (Denouement). The Complication extends to the turning-point; the Unravelling extends from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot identity requires both parts to be well-handled. Many poets tie the knot well (complication) but unravel it ill; both must be mastered. Use the turning-point to mark the reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs other kinds of tragedy (combination of elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of tragedy: the Complex (depending entirely on Reversal and Recognition), the Pathetic (motive is passion), the Ethical (motives are ethical), and the Simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should endeavour to combine as many poetic elements as possible, especially the most important ones, to create a complete tragic effect. If full combination is not possible, aim for the greatest number and most important elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of deus ex machina within the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Deus ex Machina' should be employed only for events external to the drama—for antecedent or subsequent events reported or foretold; within the action there must be nothing irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use gods or miraculous contrivances to resolve the drama's internal problems (this is appropriate only for matters beyond human knowledge). If irrational elements exist, place them outside the scope of the tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — goodness (moral purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: First and most important: character must be good. Any speech or action that manifests moral purpose will be expressive of character; the character will be good if the purpose is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness is relative to each class (a woman or slave may be 'good' within their station). Choose protagonists whose purposes can be recognized as morally directed even amid flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — propriety/appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must show propriety: traits should be appropriate to the person's sex, class, or role (e.g., manly valour is not appropriate in a woman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid indecorous or inappropriate behavior for a character's social or gender type; maintain congruence between character and expected behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — truth to life (necessity or probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must be true to life; a person of a given character should speak or act in a given way either by necessary or probable sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both complication and unraveling must arise out of the plot itself (not from external arbitrary events). Aim for actions and speeches that follow necessarily or probably from the portrayed character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character — consistency (including 'consistently inconsistent')
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourthly, character must be consistent: even if the subject that suggested the type be inconsistent, he must be consistently inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid motiveless degradation or sudden unexplained changes; inconsistency is permissible only if it itself is a consistent trait of the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of elevated types (ennobling defects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates persons above the common level; the poet should preserve the type and yet ennoble it (e.g., represent defects but make the portrait more beautiful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the example of portrait-painters: reproduce distinctive form yet improve it. Ennoble characters like Achilles to maintain tragic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and vivid visualization of scene
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructing the plot and working it out with the proper diction, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes so he sees everything with utmost vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualizing the situation helps discover what is in keeping with it and avoid inconsistencies (example: oversight in Carcinus where a character's location was implausible). Also work out appropriate gestures—natural agitation and passion make characters convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction process: general outline then episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should first sketch the general outline of the story and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General plan illustrated by Iphigenia: sketch the central action then add relevant episodes. Ensure episodes are relevant to the main action and are appropriately brief in drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes — relevance and dramatic brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes must be relevant to the action; in drama episodes are short and give extension to Epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodes to extend or diversify but keep them short and connected to the single action. Avoid extraneous incidents that do not tend to one result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an actor and integral part
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors; it should be an integral part of the whole and share in the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that pertain to other subjects and serve only as interludes (a practice criticized in later poets). Chorus should contribute to the subject like Sophocles' practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (themes and rhetorical effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought are included every effect which has to be produced by speech—the subdivisions being proof and refutation, the excitation of feelings, suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic incidents should produce effects themselves; speeches should produce their effects by what is said. Treat incidents and speeches from the same points of view to evoke pity, fear, importance, or probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and modes of utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction includes modes of utterance (commands, prayers, statements, threats, questions, answers) though delivery belongs to another art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should know the different modes and use them appropriately; ignorance of these modes is not a grave fault but knowing them aids effective dramatic speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style — clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean: clearness uses current words; a loftier style uses unusual words, metaphors, lengthening or contraction for distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance current/proper words (for clarity) with strange/rare/metaphorical/ornamental words (for distinction). Moderation is essential—overuse of rare words or metaphors produces riddles or jargon. Lengthening, contraction, and alteration can lend distinction when used judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of metaphor and rare words
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor; metaphors, strange words, and compound words have particular appropriateness to different poetic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good metaphor is the mark of genius and cannot be imparted by another; use compound words for dithyrambs, rare words for heroic poetry, metaphors for iambic. Avoid obtrusive or ludicrous use of lexical licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by tokens/signs is less artistic (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition by signs or tokens (scars, necklaces, arks) is the least artistic form and admits of more or less skilful treatment but is inferior to recognitions arising naturally from incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokens and formal proofs for purposes of plot are less desirable; prefer recognitions that are integrated with action and incident.
